texts.preamble: Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 In The Court Of District Judge (Commercial)-04, District West : Tis Hazari Courts : Delhi Cs (Comm) No. 507/2019 Cnr No. Dlwt01-8518-2019 Sakshi Mittal W/o Sh. Vineet Mittal R/o D-209, Ashok Vihar, Phase-1, New Delhi-110052.
texts.facts: Present judgement shall dispose of commercial suit for recovery of Rs. 24,04,000/- (Rupees Twenty Lakhs Four Thousands Only) alongwith interest, filed by plaintiff against the defendants. 2. The plaintiff Smt. Sakshi Mittal has filed the present suit through her husband/AR Mr. Vineet Mittal who is stated to have been authorized in this regard vide power of attorney dated 02.11.2017. It has been claimed that even otherwise husband-attorney of the plaintiff is personally aware of the facts the case. 3. As per case of plaintiff, the defendant (now defendant No. 1) M/s AAA Hospitality is a partnership firm operating through its partners. It is pleaded that in the year 2016, the defendant firm approached the plaintiff and represented that the firm was going to open a restaurant-cum-bar in the name and style of 'Raftaar' at Club Road, Punjabi Bagh and that the plaintiff would be introduced and roped in as partner of the said firm. It was told that the involvement of the plaintiff with defendant firm would bring her greater returns subject to meager investment of Rs. Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36322813/ 2 33,00,000/- which was required to be made by the plaintiff. 4. It is further pleaded by the plaintiff that after believing the representation and assurances made by the defendant to be true, the plaintiff in good faith agreed to invest a sum of Rs. 33,00,000/- for setting up of the said restaurant after which she was to be included as a partner. The amount of Rs. 33,00,000/- was paid in different installments described in para 5 of the plaint during the period from 13.06.2016 to 06.08.2016 through bank account transfer. 5. It is alleged that after receiving the entire amount of Rs. 33,00,000/- the defendant turned dishonest and failed to rope in the plaintiff as a partner as per previous assurances. The plaintiff made repeated attempts and requests to the defendant to honor its commitments but the defendant kept on delaying on one pretext or the other. Consequently, the plaintiff demanded the amount of Rs. 33,00,000/- from the defendant and then instead of paying the entire amount, the defendant paid only a sum of Rs. 10,00,000/- to the plaintiff on 26.04.2017 through bank transfer. The remaining amount of Rs. 23,00,000/- still remained unpaid. 6. It is further pleaded that on persistent reminders and requests made by the plaintiff for payment of the balance amount of Rs. 23,00,000/-, the defendant issued cheque bearing No. 000181 dated 15.07.2017 for a sum of Rs. 23,00,000/- drawn on Kotak Mahindra Bank, Netaji Subhash Place in discharge of its liability towards the plaintiff. On presentation, the said cheque was returned unpaid with remark, "Insufficient Fund" vide cheque return memo dated 21.08.2017. Complaint u/sec. 138/141/142 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 was filed by plaintiff against the defendant firm and its partners which is still pending. 7. Drawing conclusion from the conduct of the defendant it has been claimed defendant had a malafide intention of cheating and defrauding the plaintiff as neither the plaintiff was made a partner nor the amount invested by her was returned/paid back. Hence this suit for recovery of Rs. 28,04,000/- which includes the principal amount of Rs. 23,00,000/- and interest @ 12% per annum from 21.08.2017 till filing of the suit. 8. Summons of the suit were sent to the defendant firm and the same were duly served upon it. When initially suit was instituted on 16/17.10.2019 there was only one defendant i.e. the partnership firm namely M/s AAA Hospitality but later on one application u/O VI R 17 CPC was filed by plaintiff on 19.12.2022 for impleading the past and current partners of the firm in array of defendants which was allowed vide order dated 13.03.2023 and defendant No. 2 to 9 were impleaded besides the original defendant firm (now defendant No. 1). 9. Summons sent to defendant No. 5 returned back with report that Mr. Ashutosh Kanodia had expired in 2019. Hence, subsequently, name of defendant No. 5 was deleted from array of parties vide order dated 27.04.2023 on the statement of Ld. Counsel for plaintiff that he did not want to implead his LRs. Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36322813/ 3 Notwithstanding deletion of defendant No.5 from the array of the defendants, the other defendants i.e. defendant No.1 to 4 and 6 to 9 shall be referred to in this judgement by the same numbers for the sake of convenience. 10. The defendant No. 1 firm in its written statement filed under the signature of defendant No.3 has taken certain preliminary objections and denied the case of the plaintiff on merits. It is stated that the plaintiff has concealed the material facts and the suit is without cause of action. It is stated that neither the cheque in question was issued by the partners of the defendant firm nor the firm owes any contractual or other liability towards the plaintiff. It is claimed that the present partnership firm namely M/s AAA Hospitality is a reconstituted partnership firm and the erstwhile partners who had the dealings with the plaintiff are no more partners in the present firm. It is pleaded that the plaintiff has not joined/arrayed the erstwhile partnership firm named M/s AAA Hospitality having its principal place of business/registered office at A-58, Third Floor, Ashok Vihar, Phase-I, Delhi-52 nor the partners of the said firm have been made party. It is stated that there is no privity of contract between the plaintiff and the defendant firm or its partners as all dealings have taken place between the plaintiff and erstwhile partnership firm and its partners. So, an admission-cum- retirement deed dated 27.03.2018 was executed whereby Mr. Pradeep Goel, defendant No. 9 was inducted and defendant nos. 5 & 6 retired from the partnership. On 27.03.2018 itself, an MOU was executed between defendant No. 7, 8, 9 & husband of the plaintiff wherein it was stated that husband of plaintiff Mr. Vineet Mittal would get 15% share i.e. 5% & 10% respectively from share of defendant nos. 7 & 9. 18. It is further stated that by the end of third year the firm again did not make any profit and the defendant No. 8 was not willing to continue as a partner. The remaining partners decided to induct new partners, so, a deed of admission-cum-retirement dated 01.04.2019 was executed whereby the defendant No. 7 & 8 retired from the partnership firm and defendant nos. 2 Mr. Yogesh Verma and defendant No. 3 Mr. Manoj Tusir @ Manoj Kumar were inducted. With certain other facts and allegations, the defendant No. 8 has denied his liability and of the firm. Besides the preliminary objections and denial on merits, it is stated that the alleged cheque in question was issued by Mr. Ashutosh Kanodia (since expired) on 15.07.2017 i.e. prior to 23.03.2018 when the defendant No. 9 was inducted as a partner. No replication has been filed by the plaintiff to any of the written statements filed by the defendants as described above. In order to prove her case, the plaintiff examined her husband/attorney Mr. Vineet Mittal as PW-1, Mr. Swapnil Taru from Kotak Mahindra Bank as PW-2 and Mr. Piyush Goel again from Kotak Mahindra Bank as PW-3. PW-2 Mr. Swapnil Taru, a summoned witness, produced the certified copy of current bank account statement of account No. 7411750708 in the name of M/s AAA Hospitality w.e.f. 01.04.2016 to 02.11.2017 Ex.PW2/A and covering letter stating cheque bearing No. 000181 dated 15.07.2017 drawn on Kotal Mahindra Bank Ltd. is stopped by the drawer M/s AAA Hospitality Ex.PW2/B. PW-3 Mr. Piyush Goyal, another summoned witness, produced certified copy of statement of saving account No. 1011562280 in the name of Ms. Sakshi Mittal Ex.PW3/A and his authorization dated 07.10.2024 Ex.PW3/B. Thereafter, plaintiff closed her evidence. D6W1 Sh. Pankaj Gupta has relied upon Partnership Deed dated 04.04.2016 Ex.DW6/1 and Admission cum Retirement Deed dated 27.03.2018 and No due certificate Ex.PW6/2.
texts.arguments: 11. Defendant No. 2 Mr. Yogesh Verma, in his separate written statement claimed that the suit is not maintainable against him as he had joined the partnership firm on 31.03.2019 as investor/sleeping partner. Further, that it was agreed among the retiring/continuing and new partners of the defendant No. 1 firm that the defendant No. 2 would not be an active partner and would not be liable for any business liabilities, tax demands, litigation, penalties, dues etc. before the date of his joining the reconstituted firm. Further pleaded that Mr. Pradeep Goel having 35% share and Mr. Manoj Kumar having 50% share were responsible for all such liabilities. 13. The defendant No. 6 Mr. Pankaj Gupta filed a separate written statement in which several preliminary objections have been taken including the objection pertaining to bar of limitation. On merits, it is submitted that husband of the plaintiff had approached the defendant for investment of funds in the business as he was friend of the partners of the defendant firm. It is admitted that husband of the plaintiff was assured that her name would be included in the partnership business and her involvement with the defendant firm would bring greater returns and higher profits subject to investment of Rs. 33,00,000/-. It is contended that despite the assurance, the husband of the plaintiff decided not to be part of the business rather he was more interested in getting handsome return out of the investment and decided not to join the partnership as in case of her joining the partnership the plaintiff would have to share loss if any of the partnership business. Other averments made in the plaint are denied. 14. Defendant No. 7 Mr. Kunal Babuta filed his separate written statement and claimed that suit was not maintainable against him as he had retired from the firm on 31.03.2019 and it was agreed that the new partners and the retiring partners would not be responsible for any business liabilities. Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36322813/ 4 15. Defendant No. 8 Mr. Ankit Kasera, in his written statement, has claimed that plaintiff is having no cause of action against him and he is neither a necessary nor a proper party to the present suit. With certain other preliminary objections, it is stated that Mr. Ashutosh Kanodia the erstwhile defendant No. 5, who was the brother-in-law of the defendant No. 8 and accordingly he was offered to invest alongwith other investors in the bar and lounge business which was the brainchild of Sh. Vineet Mittal, the husband of the plaintiff, Pankaj Gupta (defendant No. 6) and deceased Ashutosh Kanodia (defendant No. 5). It was told that Mr. Vineet Mittal had considerable experience in the food industry and that he would manage the entire business. 16. It is pleaded in the written statement of defendant No. 8 that partnership dated 19.02.2016 was executed between defendant No. 5 Mr. Ashutosh Kanodia, defendant No. 6 Mr. Pankaj Gupta, defendant No. 7 Mr. Kunal Babuta, the plaintiff, defendant No. 8 and one Ms. Dakshi Verma who is wife of defendant No. 2. Later on, it was informed that Ms. Dakshi Verma would not continue with the partnership and the deed will have to be re-written. It is also claimed that the defendant No. 8 was told that plaintiff would not be mentioned in the new deed, however, she would continue to remain a partner for all purposes and she would introduce capital just like other partners and would be subject to profit and loss of the business and also that her husband would run the bar and lounge business. Thus, one other deed dated 04.04.2016 was executed between defendant No. 8, 5, 6 & 7, with ratio of 30:30:30:10 (10% for the defendant No. 8) however in realty the husband of the plaintiff also had a share from the share assigned to defendant nos. 5, 6 & 7 leaving the share of defendant No. 8 untouched. 17. It is also pleaded that by the end of first and second year it was conveyed that no profit could be made in the business. Further, defendant No. 5 & 6 were willing to drop out and it was conveyed that a new partner was to be inducted for more capital and to pay the outgoing partners. 30. At final argument, Ld. Counsel for plaintiff in nutshell contended that defendants did not dispute that a sum of Rs. 33 lacs was paid by plaintiff to defendant firm. He contended that defendants failed to prove that plaintiff was made partner in the firm after receipt of Rs. 33 lacs from her. He contended that it was undisputed that Rs. 10 lacs was paid back to plaintiff and a Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36322813/ 7 cheque Mark-E for Rs. 23 lacs was issued to plaintiff from defendant's firm. He contended that none of the past and current partners brought on record the books of account of the firm of the relevant period and he thus called for drawing of an adverse inference against them as books of account would have shown amount standing to the credit of the plaintiff and still unpaid to plaintiff. He further contended that none of the documents exhibited by the defendants could be said to have been proved as original thereof were never brought to the court or on record and thus they were inadmissible. He further contended that it was admitted by almost all the defendants that they neither gave public notice of retirement nor of inclusion, hence they all were liable to plaintiff being partner past and present. He further contended interse dispute about partners and proposed partner qua the business transaction qualifies as a commercial dispute. He further contended that plaintiff last legs of her fund was infused in August, 2016, she received Rs. 10 lacs in April 2017 and the cheque in question was given in July, 2017 while the present suit was filed on 16/17.10.2017 and thus the suit was well within limitation. Counsels for defendants could be summarized to the effect that plaintiff had concealed material facts as plaintiff was required to place the truth as subsequently admitted by PW1 in his cross examination and plaintiff by concealing the same from the court not only attempted to play fraud upon the court but also upon the defendants. The suit was not maintainable against the subsequently added all the partners as no pre-litigation mediation was undertaken with those subsequently added defendants. Plaintiff deliberately did not implead the partners of the firm despite being insiders of the firm as she wanted to have favourable order in their absence. PW1/husband/attorney of the plaintiff was there in the firm as late as in 2018 and if at all the then partner's of the firm were allegedly fooling the plaintiff why her husband/attorney was managing the affairs of the firm even after the alleged dishonour of the cheque which fact show that PW1 misused the cheque. The retiring partner and the new partners were not liable for the liability, if any, of the firm, in view of terms of various partnership deed retiring old partners and including new partners. Plaintiff's infusion of fund was her share of capital or that of her husband and they always remained there in firm actively. Objection qua the absence of original documents relied upon by the defendants was not sustainable in law as PW1 admitted there execution and participation. Hence, they sought dismissal of the suit. 35. Testimonies of PW1 Sh. Vineet Mittal, who is husband and attorney of plaintiff and who is otherwise claimed to be well conversant with the facts and circumstance involved in the transaction with defendant(s), as deposed by him in cross examination and relevant qua the issues involved is being put hereinafter at one place, for better appreciation. 36. PW1 Sh. Vineet Mittal, the husband/SPA of plaintiff, in his cross examination denied that plaintiff was made partner when the first partnership deed was executed in respect of Raftar Lounge and Bar. 37. PW1 further deposed that plaintiff was never into any employment and volunteered that she was into business. He further deposed that plaintiff made a company in 2012 i.e. RSV Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. engaged in restaurant and lounge business but she was no longer director in the said company as she resigned probably in the year 2015. His wife resigned from another company namely Akashdeep Hospitality only after few months. He deposed that he had been a partner in a business firm which was engaged in construction work but he did not remember the name of the said firm, though they were four partners in the said firm. He deposed that in respect of defendant No.1 the partners namely Ashutosh Kanoida, Pankaj Gupta, Yogesh Verma and Kunal Babuta had approached him to become partner in the said firm. 38. He deposed that infusion of Rs. 33 lacs in the firm was not a friendly loan but an investment in the firm in lieu of plaintiff becoming partner in the firm. He denied the suggestion that it was his idea to open restaurant cum lounge cum bar with the erstwhile partners named above. He denied the suggestion that he was managing the affairs of the restaurant cum lunge cum bar but deposed that he was managing the affairs alongwith other partners named above. He deposed that plaintiff was not involved in the management of the affairs but the firm was running good when he was involved with the same. He volunteered that he remained involved with the management of the firm only for a limited period when the construction was being done (later he admitted that he was called by police as partner when a murder had taken place in restaurant in 2018) , and all the accounts were handled by Ashuthosh Kanodia. 59. In Kailash Devi Khanna v. DD Global Capital Ltd. 2019 SCC Online Del 9954 Hon'ble Delhi High Court emphasized that not all suits for monetary recovery qualify as "commercial dispute" under the Act of 2015. The Court specifically observed that for a claim to fall under Section 2(1)(c)(i) of the Act of 2015, it must pertain to "ordinary transactions of merchants, bankers, financiers, and traders," involving mercantile documents and their enforcement or interpretation. The Court further held that a suit merely seeking recovery of money, without any connection to mercantile transactions or documents, does not meet the criteria of a "commercial dispute" and, therefore, cannot be filed as a commercial suit. 60. Interse dispute between the merchants, banker, financier and traders qua transaction connected with their business do qualify as "commercial dispute".
